lead: A clutch is a friction joint you can switch on and off. It lets a running engine take up the load of a stationary gearbox without shock. A brake is the same joint with one side held still: it turns kinetic energy into heat until the wheel stops. Both are judged by the torque they carry and by the heat their rubbing surfaces can absorb. You meet them in a motorcycle, a car, a lathe, a lift and a train.
prereq: You need friction, power as torque × angular speed and unit conversion from Unit 1, plus shaft torque from Chapter 3.1; torque flow through a drivetrain is in Chapter 3.4.

sections.h3: One plate, many plates, and what slips

blocks.text: A coupling joins two shafts permanently. A clutch joins them only when you ask it to. Press the pedal and the engine spins free of the gearbox; release it and friction drags both sides to the same speed. That dragging is slip, and slip is deliberate: it lets a car start from rest without a jolt.

The rubbing parts sit in a stack. In a single-plate clutch a steel plate carries friction lining on both faces. A spring pushes it against the flywheel on one side and the pressure plate on the other, so two rubbing pairs share the axial force W, the spring force in newtons. Find the torque for one pair, then multiply by the number of pairs.

Count every friction surface, including the flywheel face and the pressure-plate face. A stack of p such members gives p − 1 rubbing pairs; the familiar single plate lined on both faces, clamped between flywheel and pressure plate, is three members and so gives 2 pairs. Stack more plates and the same W buys more torque, which keeps motorcycle and machine-tool clutches short. Running the plates in oil keeps them cool and quiet: a wet clutch.

A cone clutch replaces flat faces with a shallow cone, so the wedge effect gives a larger normal force for the same W. A centrifugal clutch lets spring-loaded shoes fly outward as speed rises and engages by itself, which is why small scooters have no clutch lever.

Friction torque depends on how the pressure is spread over the ring between r_i, the inner radius in metres, and r_o, the outer radius in metres. Two assumptions are used; take the one the question names.

A new clutch has pressure nearly uniform over the face. Wear rate goes as pressure × sliding speed, and sliding speed is ωr, so the outer lining wears fastest. After running in, the face settles into a state where pressure × radius is constant — uniform wear — and the highest pressure then sits at r_i, the smallest radius.

blocks.where: T is the friction torque per rubbing pair in N·m; μ is the coefficient of friction (no unit); W is the axial force in N; r_o and r_i are outer and inner radii in m.

blocks.text: A clutch that is new, or rarely used, has not worn into shape, so its pressure is nearly uniform over the face.

blocks.where: the symbols are as above; the radii are in m and the bracket has units of m, so T comes out in N·m per rubbing pair.

blocks.text: Both formulas assume μ is constant across the face. Uniform pressure gives slightly more torque than uniform wear for the same W and radii. Use uniform wear for any clutch in service, and for brakes almost always. Multiply by n, the number of rubbing pairs: a single-plate clutch has n = 2.

sections.h3: Brakes: friction with one side held still

blocks.text: A brake holds one friction member still. The drum or disc turns with the wheel; the block or pad is fixed to the frame and pushed on by a lever, cam or hydraulic piston. The torque relation is the same: T = μ N r, with N the normal force on the drum in N and r the drum radius in m.

A block brake is a lever with a block pressing one spot of the drum. Moments about the lever pivot give N, so the lever lengths set the braking torque. If the friction force helps apply the block, the brake is self-energizing; pushed too far it becomes self-locking and will not release.

A shoe brake curves the lining around a larger arc of the drum, so the same pressure gives more torque; scooter and truck drum brakes work this way. A disc brake presses flat pads on a rotating disc, with r taken at the mean radius of the pad.
Every stop turns kinetic energy into heat in the lining and drum. For steady slipping:

blocks.where: E is the heat generated in J; T is the friction torque in N·m; Δω is the relative angular speed between the two members in rad/s; t is the slip time in s.

blocks.text: That heat must first be stored in the drum and lining, then carried away by air. When it cannot, the lining gets hot, μ falls and the brake fades — a real worry on a long downhill run. Brakes are sized by energy per stop and by how often stops repeat, not by torque alone.

figure.caption: Torque from the engine crosses the clutch to the gearbox and the wheel; the brake acts on the wheel and turns its motion into heat. Clutch and brake are the same friction idea, one joining two spinning parts and one stopping them.

examples.question: A single-plate clutch has outer radius 150 mm and inner radius 100 mm. The coefficient of friction is 0.3 and the axial force is 5 kN. Find the torque capacity by uniform wear theory. Find the power transmitted at 1200 rpm. Estimate the heat per engagement if the clutch slips for 0.5 s, starting at a relative speed of 600 rpm.
steps: Convert to SI: r_o = 0.15 m, r_i = 0.10 m, W = 5000 N.
Count the rubbing pairs: a single plate lined on both faces, clamped between flywheel and pressure plate, gives n = 2.
Torque per pair: T₁ = μ W (r_o + r_i)/2 = 0.3 × 5000 × 0.125 = 187.5 N·m.

The friction torque stays roughly constant, but the relative speed falls linearly from 62.83 rad/s to zero, so the mean relative speed is half the initial value. E ≈ T (Δω/2) t = 375 × 62.83 × 0.5 × 0.5 ≈ 5890 J.
examples.answer: The clutch carries 375 N·m, transmits about 47.1 kW at 1200 rpm, and each engagement turns about 5.9 kJ into heat.
examples.check:
import math
mu = 0.3
W = 5000.0
ro = 0.15
ri = 0.10
n = 2
T1 = mu * W * (ro + ri) / 2
T = n * T1
print(round(T, 1))
omega = 2 * math.pi * 1200 / 60
print(round(T * omega, 1))
domega = 2 * math.pi * 600 / 60
print(round(T * domega * 0.5 * 0.5, 1))
examples.output: E = T Δω t is right only for steady slipping, as when a brake holds a constant speed.

traps: Using the uniform pressure formula on a worn-in clutch, and forgetting the number of rubbing pairs — a single-plate clutch has n = 2, not 1.
Putting millimetres straight into the torque formula. T comes out in N·m only when the radii are in metres.
In uniform wear, the maximum pressure is at the inner radius, not the outer one; the worn face has p r = constant.
Quoting engine speed where relative speed is needed. During a gear change the slip speed is the difference of the two side speeds, and it falls to zero.
For a block brake, forgetting that the normal force N comes from lever moments about the pivot, not from the force you apply on the pedal.

quiz.q: State the uniform wear torque formula for one pair of friction surfaces and define every symbol.
quiz.a: T = μ W (r_o + r_i)/2, where μ is the coefficient of friction, W the axial force in N, r_o the outer radius in m and r_i the inner radius in m; T is in N·m.

quiz.q: Why is uniform wear theory preferred for a clutch that has been in service?
quiz.a: The outer part wears faster until the face settles into a state where pressure × radius is constant. The lining then has its highest pressure at the inner radius, which is what the uniform wear formula assumes. Uniform pressure fits only a new, flat, rarely used clutch.

quiz.q: A multi-plate clutch has 4 rubbing pairs, μ = 0.25, axial force 4 kN, r_o = 120 mm and r_i = 80 mm. Find the torque capacity by uniform wear theory.
Write the braking torque of a block brake on a drum and say where the normal force comes from.
quiz.a: T = μ N r, with N the normal force in N and r the drum radius in m. N is found by taking moments about the lever pivot, so the lever arms set the braking torque.

quiz.q: A brake absorbs 300 N·m while the relative speed is 100 rad/s, and the stop takes 0.4 s. Find the heat generated per stop.
quiz.a: E = T Δω t = 300 × 100 × 0.4 = 12000 J, that is 12 kJ per stop.

quiz.q: For the same axial force and the same radii, which theory gives the higher torque and why?
quiz.a: Uniform pressure gives the higher torque. In uniform wear the pressure piles up at the inner radius, where the moment arm of the friction force is small. Spreading the same total force uniformly outward puts more of it at larger radius, so the torque is slightly higher.

quiz.q: A truck on a long downhill grade loses braking force after repeated use. Explain the cause in terms of the chapter's equations.
quiz.a: Each second of dragging puts E = T Δω t joules into the lining and drum. Repeated stops give the drum no time to shed that heat to the air, so its temperature rises. Hot lining material has a lower μ, so T = μ N r falls and the driver must press harder; this is brake fade. Fixes are larger lining area, better cooling and engine braking.

beyond: Not for the exam. Wet multi-plate clutches inside dual-clutch gearboxes run in oil and are worked by hydraulics in milliseconds, so the slip time t in E = T Δω t is a control variable, not a fixed number. Electric vehicles recover much of the braking energy instead of turning it all into heat, so their friction brakes are sized for the rare hard stop. Carbon-ceramic discs and sintered linings survive high energy per stop without fade. To go further, look up clutch lining friction coefficient versus temperature, brake fade testing, and regenerative braking blend strategies.
